title: The Pastoral Letters
aka: the letters to Timothy and Titus
lead: 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are three letters in Paul's name to two coworkers left to lead churches, Timothy in Ephesus and Titus on Crete. Since the 1700s they have been called the "Pastoral" letters because they deal with the care of churches: leaders, sound teaching, households and false teachers. Who wrote them, and when, is one of the most argued questions about the New Testament.

sections.b:
The three letters share words and concerns found little or nowhere else in Paul: "sound teaching" (1 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 4:3; Titus 1:9), "godliness" (1 Timothy 2:2; 4:7-8; 6:6; 2 Timothy 3:5; Titus 1:1), the "appearing" of Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 6:14; 2 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13), God "our Savior" (1 Timothy 1:1; 2:3; Titus 1:3; Titus 2:10; Titus 3:4), and the formula "This saying is trustworthy" (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). Each is written to one man, but each also expects to be read to a church: all three close with grace to "you" in the plural (1 Timothy 6:21; 2 Timothy 4:22; Titus 3:15).

1 Timothy and Titus are mostly instructions: who may lead, how households and groups in the church should live, what to do about teachers who have gone wrong. 2 Timothy reads as a farewell from a prisoner who expects to die.

sections.h: Who wrote them: the traditional view
sections.b:
The letters name Paul as their writer (1 Timothy 1:1; 2 Timothy 1:1; Titus 1:1), and the church read them as his from the second century on. Irenaeus opens his work Against Heresies (about AD 180) by warning against "vain genealogies", "as the apostle says" (1 Timothy 1:4), and Polycarp's letter to the Philippians has lines very close to 1 Timothy 6:7, 10; scholars rate his use of 1 Timothy from a "high probability" (Holmes) to "certain" (Hartog). Those who hold that Paul wrote them usually place them after the end of Acts: Paul was released from his first Roman imprisonment (Acts 28:30-31), traveled again in the east, and was arrested and killed in a second imprisonment. Eusebius (Church History 2.22, about AD 325) tells it that way, saying Paul "was sent again upon the ministry of preaching" and wrote 2 Timothy in the later imprisonment, and 1 Clement 5 (about AD 96) says Paul reached "the extreme limit of the west" before his death.

Defenders answer the critical case point by point. Style and vocabulary: letters to trusted coworkers about church order, written late in life against new opponents, would sound different from letters to young churches, and Luke Timothy Johnson has made a searching criticism of the methods used to decide authorship; Stanley Porter and Ray Van Neste hold that the differences in language match the differences in the readers. A secretary may have shaped the wording (E. Randolph Richards has argued for the part secretaries played in Paul's letters; Ben Witherington: "the voice is the voice of Paul, but the hand is the hand of Luke"). The many personal details, especially in 2 Timothy 4:9-21, read more naturally as real than as invented. Commentators who argue for Paul's authorship include Johnson (Anchor Bible) and Philip Towner (New International Commentary on the New Testament), and J. N. D. Kelly and Gordon Fee in their commentaries; Robert Yarbrough is a recent defender.

sections.h: Who wrote them: the critical view
sections.b: Friedrich Schleiermacher questioned 1 Timothy in 1807; since then most critical scholars have come to hold that a follower of Paul wrote all three after his death, in his name and with his authority. Proposed dates range from the late first century to the middle of the second. Their reasons: the vocabulary and style differ from the undisputed letters (P. N. Harrison's 1921 study of the vocabulary began the modern statistical argument); "faith" often means a body of teaching to be guarded (1 Timothy 6:20) rather than trust; church leadership has settled offices with qualifications; the opponents look like later teachers, and some scholars read the letters as answers to second-century movements such as Marcion's; and the travels the letters assume (1 Timothy 1:3; Titus 1:5) are hard to fit into Paul's life as Acts and his other letters tell it. I. Howard Marshall (International Critical Commentary) concludes that Paul did not write them, and James Dunn treats them as written in Paul's name; Lewis Donelson's study is a standard statement of the case against Paul's authorship. A middle way holds that genuine fragments of Paul were worked into later letters, especially in 2 Timothy. Each book page gives the views with their arguments; this site follows the text as written ("Paul") and labels the question.

If a follower wrote the letters, was that honest? Views differ. (1) An accepted practice: Richard Bauckham has argued that writing in a revered figure's name was not normally forgery or deceit in early Judaism and Christianity. (2) Allonymity: I. Howard Marshall prefers this word, "authorship by another person": a disciple, with no intent to deceive, voicing what he believed Paul would say after his death; Philip Towner gives this proposal more room than other critical theories. (3) Deception: Bart Ehrman (Forgery and Counterforgery, 2012) argues that ancient critics, pagan, Jewish and Christian, treated false claims of authorship as literary deceit, so that modern attempts to excuse such writings are misplaced. (4) Paul wrote them: for those who hold Paul's authorship, with or without a secretary, the question does not arise. The church's own later practice is part of the argument: works it judged falsely ascribed were rejected when the judgment was made.

The oldest surviving collection of Paul's letters, the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), has lost its last leaves, so no one can see whether it held the Pastorals. Frederic Kenyon, its first editor, counted the missing pages and judged there was not room for them; others answer that the scribe could have added leaves, so the question stays open. Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.21) says that Marcion, the second-century teacher who made his own short canon of Paul, rejected the two letters to Timothy and the one to Titus. Some scholars read that as Marcion cutting letters he knew; others as a sign the letters were not yet widely known; a few think the letters were written partly to answer Marcion (1 Timothy 6:20).

The letters name overseers (1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:7-9), elders (1 Timothy 5:17-19; Titus 1:5), deacons (1 Timothy 3:8-13), and an enrolled group of widows (1 Timothy 5:3-16). In Titus 1:5-7 "elders" and "overseer" seem to name the same leaders, as in Acts 20:17, 28. The lists ask more about character and household than about gifts: married once, sober, hospitable, able to teach, not a lover of money. Later churches built three different orders on these chapters (bishops over elders and deacons; elders governing together; congregations choosing their own pastors and deacons), and the topic pages on elders and deacons set them side by side.
